Where it began

Darren Lehmann was born in Gawler, South Australia, on 5 February 1970, and went to school there. As a boy he played junior Australian rules football for Central District as well as cricket. At 16 he left school for a job on the Holden assembly line in Elizabeth, and he liked factory life enough to turn down a place in the first intake of the new Australian Cricket Academy.

Cricket came looking for him anyway. He played his first game for South Australia at 17, at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, and at 19 he made 228 against New South Wales.

The player

He was a busy, attacking left-handed batsman with a style all his own: he took guard outside leg stump and shuffled right across as the bowler ran in. It worked. He made mountains of runs in Australia and in England, but in a very strong Australian side he had to be patient. His Test debut came in Bangalore in March 1998, and he marked it with 52 and the wicket of India's captain.

In 27 Tests he made 1,798 runs at 44.95, with 5 hundreds and a best of 177. He also took 15 wickets with his flat left-arm spin. His finest stretch came in 2003 and 2004, when he made back-to-back hundreds against Bangladesh and then again in Sri Lanka, where Australia won all three Tests. He also played in two World Cup wins: he hit the winning runs in the 1999 final and held the catch that ended the 2003 one.

What made him special

Spin bowling held few fears for him, and in county cricket he was close to unstoppable. For Yorkshire, between 1997 and 2006, he scored 8871 Championship runs at 68.76 and helped them to the 2001 title. In his last game for the club he made 339 against Durham, the highest first-class innings ever played at Headingley, passing a 334 made there by Don Bradman in 1930.

At home he was just as prolific. By the time he retired, in 2007, nobody had made more runs in the Sheffield Shield.

Away from the middle

After playing he became a coach, winning the IPL with the Deccan Chargers in 2009 and the Sheffield Shield with Queensland. He coached Australia from 2013, through a 5–0 Ashes win in 2013–14 and the 2015 World Cup triumph. He later coached in the Big Bash League and The Hundred, and in October 2024 took charge of Northamptonshire. Wisden named him a Cricketer of the Year, and his son Jake went on to play first-class cricket.

And finally

In 2012 a statue of him by the sculptor Ken Martin was put up at Adelaide Oval. Not bad for a man who once preferred building cars to a place at the Academy.
